# OneApp (also known as "One App")

> OneApp — every tool in one place. Sketch notes, a full PDF editor, image studio, todos, reminders, timer and more. A single free offline-first (PWA) web workspace at https://oneappready.vercel.app; all data stays local in the browser, no sign-up.

## Apps

- [Sketch Notes](/): freehand drawing and note canvas
- [PDF Editor](/pdfeditor): view, edit, annotate and organize PDFs
- [Image Studio](/image): image editing and adjustments
- [Board](/board): a personal page the user composes **by prompting**. One text field takes plain-English instructions and a local, deterministic parser (no network, no API key, no model) turns each one into a single board edit. Five section types — **Note** (free text), **Checklist** (tickable rows), **Counter** (a tally with an optional goal, step and unit), **Links** (saved `http(s)` addresses) and **Habit** (a seven-day local-calendar streak). The grammar covers add ("add a checklist for groceries", "add a counter for water with a goal of 8", "add a note called Ideas"), modify ("rename groceries to shopping", "set the water goal to 10", "set the water unit to glasses", "turn ideas into a checklist", "make ideas wide", "move groceries to top", "collapse ideas"), fill in ("add milk to groceries", "add docs example.com to work", "check milk", "add 5 to water", "check today on reading") and remove ("remove milk from groceries", "remove groceries", "reset water", "clear the board", "undo"). References resolve by title, then loosely, then by type name, and an ambiguous or unknown reference is answered with which sections exist rather than a silent no-op; every phrasing is published in an in-app "What you can say" sheet whose lines are tappable and live. Every command has an equivalent direct control on the card (add-type bar, inline title editing, +/−, tick, move, width, reset, remove, change type), so the app is fully usable without composing a sentence. Undo covers the last 25 changes for the session. Fully offline; the board is stored in this browser under `sknotes:board` and never uploaded
- [Todos](/todos): task list and planner, framed five ways. **Agenda** is the one that answers "what is coming": it gathers **tasks and reminders together** — merged at the shell (`lib/schedule.ts`) so neither app reaches into the other — and groups them by distance from now rather than by calendar unit: overdue (oldest first, since that is the one to deal with), today, tomorrow, the rest of this week, next week, later, undated, and what was finished in the last seven days. A repeating reminder that has already fired is *upcoming*, not done. Tasks stay tickable and editable inline; reminders are shown as they will fire and are changed in their own app. **Day / Week / Month / Year** frame the same tasks by calendar period, with a stepper the agenda does not have because it spans every date.
- [Reminders](/reminders): scheduled reminders with notifications
- [Timer](/timer): pomodoro and countdown timer
- [System Info](/system): live device and system dashboard — OS, processor, memory, graphics, display, battery, network, storage, locale and the browser capability matrix, as live meters plus an exportable report. Carries a compact nearby-devices panel; the full scanner is its own app, below
- [Resource Monitor](/resources): see what is using this device, and which app is doing it. Four views. **Live** — the consent-gated resources shown by holding them: open the **camera** or a **screen capture** and a live preview plays with the source name, format and a running timer; open the **microphone** and a live level meter moves; start a **location watch** and every fix, its accuracy and the update count appear as they arrive. One button releases each. Beside them, live meters for the resources that need no permission at all — JS heap against its ceiling, storage against the origin quota, processor cores and frame rate, battery level and charging, connection type/downlink/round-trip, bytes pulled over the network since load, and display size. **Access** — all twenty resources a page can ask for, each with this browser's live answer (allowed / blocked / asks first / not available), what it would let a site do, and which apps here would ever use it: camera, microphone, screen recording, speaker choice, location, notifications, clipboard read and write, screen wake lock, idle detection, window placement, installed fonts, motion sensors, MIDI, Bluetooth, USB, HID, serial ports, persistent storage and cross-site cookies. States update live from the Permissions API, so a change made in the browser's own site settings appears without a refresh, and the ones that can be asked for safely have an "Ask for it now" button that releases immediately. **Apps** — the single browser origin broken back into every app behind it, which is the view a browser's site settings cannot produce: per app, the resources it can reach, whether it sends anything over the network and what for, and the bytes it is actually holding in this browser (attributed by walking the storage key scheme), filterable by camera-or-mic, network and stores-data. **Privacy** — Do Not Track, Global Privacy Control, secure context, cookie and automation state; every host the page has actually contacted with its request count and bytes, first- and third-party separated, read from the browser's own Resource Timing log; what is kept on the device (saved data and key count, offline caches and file count, readable cookies, IndexedDB databases, persistence state); and the identity surface — user agent, languages, time zone, screen, window, cores, device memory, touch points, colour scheme and motion preference — everything readable by any site with no prompt at all. The app is strictly read-only: it writes nothing, deletes nothing and uploads nothing, and anything it opens is released the moment you switch apps. It reports on the OneApp workspace only — a web page cannot see what other tabs or other applications are doing with the camera, microphone or screen, and the app says so rather than implying otherwise. Fully offline
- [Nearby Devices](/nearby): find the hardware around this machine and read what each piece of it is. Discovery uses every route the web platform allows — devices this site was already granted over **Web Bluetooth, WebUSB, WebHID and Web Serial**, attached microphones, speakers and cameras, connected game controllers, cast-capable displays on the local network via the Presentation API, and (on Chrome with experimental web features enabled) a **live BLE advertisement scan** streaming every broadcast in range with its signal strength. A page cannot sweep the airwaves by itself: each transport button opens the *browser's own* chooser, and only the device the user picks becomes visible to the app — attached audio, video and controller hardware needs no prompt. An **Available to connect** section then lists every Bluetooth, USB, HID and serial device that can hold a link, each with a Connect button, live link state, elapsed connected time and Disconnect; serial ports take a chosen baud rate (9600–921600) before opening. Connecting means a GATT connection on Bluetooth, a WebUSB session with a configuration selected (no interface claimed) on USB, an open handle on HID, and a reserved port on serial — no data is written on any transport, and every link is closed on disconnect or when the page is left. Selecting a device opens its full sheet, read from the descriptor the platform already returned, without opening or claiming anything: **USB** — manufacturer, product, vendor/product ids, device class/subclass/protocol translated to names, USB and device revisions, and every configuration with its interfaces, alternates and endpoints (direction, transfer type, packet size); **HID** — vendor/product ids, the collection tree with usage pages and usages named, and the input/output/feature report layout; **serial** — USB vendor/product ids behind the port; **cameras and microphones** — the track capabilities the hardware advertises (resolutions, frame rates, facing mode, sample rate, channels, echo cancellation and the rest) once the site holds camera/mic permission; **controllers** — layout plus a live view of every button pressure and stick axis, which doubles as a gamepad tester. **Bluetooth** features need a live link, so a per-device "Connect & read features" action walks the GATT table — every primary service and characteristic with what it permits, plus manufacturer name, model number, firmware/hardware/software revision, appearance, transmit power and battery level — then disconnects again. A browser-support matrix shows which of the eight discovery APIs exist here, and the whole inventory copies out as a plain-text report. Fully offline (the APIs are local); everything is read on-device and nothing is transmitted
- [Speed Test](/speedtest): network speed measurement
- [News](/news): latest headlines by category — tech, software engineering, sports, national, international, state (Kerala) and local
- [Streams](/streams): play music and live channels from YouTube inside the workspace. Four sections. **Music** — curated stations by genre and language scene (Lo-fi, Top hits, Bollywood, Malayalam, Tamil, Chill, Instrumental, Classical, Jazz, Rock, EDM, Devotional). **Live** — what is broadcasting right now: music radio, lo-fi radio, world and India and Malayalam news, sports, nature, space, study rooms, gaming. **Search** — anything on YouTube, filtered to everything, music only, or live only. **Library** — videos saved from any card and a trail of the last two dozen played, both stored in this browser (`sknotes:streams:*`) and never uploaded, clearable in the app. Each station is a saved *search*, never a pinned video id, so a station keeps working as streams start and end. Finding is done server-side by this site's own `/api/streams` route, which runs the search and returns only the two dozen small records a grid draws; the browser never talks to youtube.com directly. Playing is done by YouTube's own privacy-enhanced embed (`youtube-nocookie.com`) on YouTube's domain, so the creator's view is counted and YouTube's terms apply unchanged — nothing is downloaded, proxied or re-hosted. The player shrinks to a bar while browsing without interrupting playback, and is unmounted when you leave the app, so audio never follows you into another one. Needs a connection.
- [World Clock](/worldclock): live time anywhere in the world, and the country behind each clock. Three views over one selection. **Clocks** — your own time leads a board of pinned cities (120+ cities across 68 countries and every inhabited time zone, including half- and quarter-hour offsets like India's UTC+05:30 and Nepal's UTC+05:45); each card shows the live time, the zone abbreviation, the offset relative to you, a "Tomorrow"/"Yesterday" badge whenever the date differs, a day/night glyph and a plain-language read on whether it is a reasonable hour to call. A time-shift slider moves every clock together by up to ±12 hours for planning a call or meeting across zones. Cities are searchable by name, former name, country, capital, ISO code or IANA zone ("bombay", "kerala", "GB", "asia/kolkata" all work) and the pinned board persists on the device. **Country** — capital, region, population (approximate, with density), area, currency and symbol, official languages, international dialling code, which side of the road it drives on, internet TLD and current UTC offset, plus a short profile and what the country is known for (its specialities), and the live local time in each of its cities. **News** — latest headlines from that country's own news edition in English. Time zones are computed with the browser's `Intl` API, so daylight saving always follows the platform's current tz database; the clocks, country details and specialities are all bundled and work fully offline, and only the headlines need a connection
- [Malayalam Writer](/malayalam): write Malayalam by transliteration (Manglish), an on-screen keyboard, or handwriting
- [Translate](/translate): translate text between languages, online (auto-detects the source) or fully offline on-device via the browser's built-in AI — no text leaves the device
- [Morse Code](/morse): learn, practise and send International Morse code. Four tools — a tappable chart of every letter, number, punctuation mark and prosign; a four-choice drill that weights unseen and shaky characters and tracks per-character mastery; a text ⇄ Morse translator that plays the message; and a straight key you hold to send, decoded live from your own timing. Speed (5–30 WPM) and sidetone pitch are adjustable, and every signal plays as sound, an on-screen lamp and optional vibration. Fully offline — the tone is synthesized with the Web Audio API, so no audio files are downloaded
- [Sound Meter](/soundmeter): measure sound from the microphone. Four readings from one live analysis — the fundamental frequency in Hz (autocorrelation, 50 Hz–2 kHz) alongside the loudest tone present; the nearest musical note with its cents error, making it a working instrument tuner (reference A adjustable 415–444 Hz); loudness as RMS and peak dBFS with a session peak hold, a clipping warning and an adjustable — explicitly uncalibrated — dB SPL estimate; and a live visualization that switches between a 20 Hz–20 kHz log-scale FFT spectrum (pointing at a peak reads out its frequency and note) and a time-domain waveform scope. Fully offline via the Web Audio API. Requires microphone permission; no audio is recorded, stored or transmitted, each frame is analysed and discarded, and the microphone is released on stopping or switching apps
- [Color Lens](/color): identify any colour in a picture. Attach an image, drop or paste one, or take a photo with the device camera (in-app viewfinder with front/rear switching, falling back to the system camera app), then tap, drag or arrow-key anywhere on it; a pixel-level loupe magnifies the sample point and the sample size is switchable between 1 px, 3×3 and 5×5 averaging. Every reading is reported in full — HEX (with the short form), RGB, HSL, HSB/HSV, CMYK, CIE L*a*b*, LCH, XYZ and WCAG relative luminance — alongside the nearest of the 148 CSS colour names (matched by ΔE in L*a*b*), perceived brightness, a warm/cool read, and contrast ratios against white and black graded to WCAG 2.2 AA, AA-large and AAA with live text samples. It also extracts the image's dominant palette by median cut (4, 6, 8 or 12 swatches, each with the share of the picture it covers) plus the overall average colour, and derives complementary, analogous, triadic, split-complementary, tetradic and monochromatic schemes and a nine-step tint/shade ramp from whatever is picked. Palettes export as a hex list, CSS variables, a Tailwind v4 `@theme` block, SCSS variables or JSON. A hex code can be typed in directly instead of read from a photo, recent picks are kept on the device, and on Chromium the browser's EyeDropper API adds picking from anywhere on screen. Fully offline — the image is decoded and sampled in the browser and is never uploaded
- [QR Codes](/qr): read and write QR codes, entirely on this device. **Scan** with the camera (the browser's own barcode detector where it exists, a bundled decoder where it does not, so every browser here can read one), or from a picture that already has a code in it: choose a file, drop it, or paste a screenshot, with no camera permission involved at all. A reading is always shown in full before anything is acted on, and only http(s), mailto: and tel: destinations are ever made clickable — a printed code is untrusted input. **Create** the kinds a phone camera actually acts on, in their real formats: plain text, links, Wi-Fi credentials (WIFI: with security type and hidden-network flag), email (mailto: with subject and body), phone (tel:), SMS (SMSTO:), a location (geo:) and a contact card (vCard 3.0) — with a live preview, four error-correction levels, a byte-capacity readout and PNG or SVG export. Codes scanned and made are kept on the device (up to 40) and clearable from the app or from Settings → Data. The camera is released the moment scanning stops or the app is left, and no frame is ever stored or transmitted
- [Handoff](/handoff): move what this browser holds onto another device with nothing in between — no account, no upload, no cable. Pick per app what to send (each row shows its size), then hold the screen up to the other device: the data is compressed, split across as many QR codes as it needs and played as a loop, and the receiving device reads them in any order until it has a complete, checksummed set. For larger data a **direct link** uses the same codes to exchange WebRTC connection details (an offer one way, an answer back) and then transfers everything at once over the local network — no STUN or TURN server is configured, so nothing leaves the network and a link only works between two devices on it. What travels is exactly the backup document Settings → Data writes to a file, so it is validated by the same reader and lands through the same add-or-replace choice; nothing is written until it is accepted
- [Clone](/clone): copy one device's **entire** workspace onto another — every app's data and every setting — down whichever route the two devices actually have. This is the whole-device operation; Handoff is the same idea for one or two chosen apps. **By cable** — plug the devices together and turn on USB tethering, and the wire becomes a private network the direct link runs inside, so a full clone crosses in seconds with no router, no internet and no third party involved at all; where a cable can't carry a network, the clone is written as a file onto a USB drive or memory card and read back on the other side. **Over a network** — the same direct link on one Wi-Fi (contacting nothing outside it), or between two different networks, which is the one case that asks a public STUN server what address this device looks like from outside; it never sees the clone, and there is no relay anywhere. **Without a network** — the clone becomes a loop of QR codes read straight off this screen by the other device's camera, with no radio of any kind. The two devices are introduced by the user rather than by a signalling server: the connection code travels as a QR code, as a link (the code sits after the # so it never reaches a server), or as a token pasted into any chat app, and the far end answers the same way. What travels is the same document Settings → Data writes to a backup file, wrapped with the sending device's name, when it was taken, and a checksum over exactly those bytes — so a backup can be cloned onto a device and a clone can be kept as a backup, and a clone that arrived short or damaged is **refused rather than half-applied**. On the wire the payload is deflated and moved in chunks sized to what the connection negotiated, with backpressure, and the receiver is told the total up front so its progress is a real fraction. **Nothing is written until the arriving clone has been described**: the receiving device shows where it came from, what it holds app by app, and a row per app saying what would happen here — arrives, replaced, untouched, or deleted — under either of two choices: add it alongside what is already on this device, or make this device identical, which deletes anything the clone doesn't carry and says how many items that is before the button is pressed. Once written, a receipt travels back so the sending device — usually the one about to be wiped — knows what actually landed
- [File Drop](/drop): send files of any size from any device to any device, with nothing in between. Queue files (drag, drop or choose — nothing is read until the transfer starts, so a multi-gigabyte video costs no memory to queue), pick how far the connection has to reach, and hand the other device an invite. **This network only** contacts nothing outside the network at all and works with no internet connection; **anywhere** asks a public STUN server what address this device looks like from outside — it never sees the files — which is what lets two devices on different networks connect. The introduction is done by the user rather than by a signalling server: the invite travels as a QR code, as a link (the code sits after the # so it never reaches a server), or as a token pasted into any chat app, and the receiving device hands back a reply the same way. Once connected, files stream over a WebRTC data channel a chunk at a time, sized to what the connection negotiated (up to 256 KB). **Nothing is ever held whole, at either end**, which is what makes a multi-gigabyte file work: the sender reads each file a slice at a time from disk with one chunk read ahead, and the receiver writes each chunk straight out — into a folder it picks (Chromium: no size limit, and the only sink that can resume), or as a *streaming* download where there is no folder picker, which hands the service worker a stream that the browser writes to disk as it arrives (Firefox, Safari: also no size limit). Only where neither exists does it fall back to collecting a file in memory first, and it says so before the transfer starts rather than after it fails. **Backpressure runs in both directions** — the channel's own buffer governs the wire, and the receiver tells the sender to pause when its disk falls behind, which is what stops a fast link filling memory on a large file. **An interrupted transfer resumes**: with a folder sink the partial file is on disk, so a fresh invite continues from the byte it stopped at, with both sides re-hashing the prefix so the whole-file checksum still holds. Every file carries a CRC-32 computed as the bytes fly past and is verified on arrival — a file that doesn't match is discarded rather than saved. The screen is held awake for the duration, progress, throughput and time remaining are shown throughout, either side can stop, and there is no relay server: a small share of network pairs behind strict carrier NAT cannot be connected directly, and the app says exactly that and points at the same-network route instead of failing vaguely
- [Text Kit](/text): the small operations on text, done on this device instead of on a stranger's website. Six tools over **one shared draft** — so they compose (decode a payload, format the JSON inside it, diff it against yesterday's) and the draft is kept, because what people paste into a text tool is usually mid-task. **Text** — upper, lower, title, sentence, camel, Pascal, snake and kebab case (word boundaries found inside identifiers, so parseHTMLDocument becomes parse_html_document), plus sort A→Z, Z→A and naturally (file2 before file10), remove duplicates, reverse, trim, drop blank lines, number the lines, and live counts of characters, characters without spaces, words, lines, paragraphs, UTF-8 bytes and reading time. **Encode** — base64 (standard and URL-safe), URL and URL-component escaping, HTML entities and JSON string quoting, in both directions, live, UTF-8 safe (so Malayalam and emoji round-trip), with a failure *explained* rather than a blank box. **JSON** — format at 2, 4 or tab indent, minify, and sort keys at every depth so two documents can be compared line by line; an invalid document is reported by line, column and what was expected, with the offending line quoted, using its own validator rather than scraping the browser's error message. **Compare** — a line diff with add/remove attribution, line numbers on both sides, changed-lines-only view, and a graceful degrade on very large inputs rather than freezing. **Regex** — pattern and flags with live matches, capture groups, named groups and a replacement preview supporting $1, $& and $<name>; a bad pattern is a message, and the subject is capped so a pathological pattern cannot hang the tab. **Hash** — SHA-1/256/384/512 and CRC-32 of text or of a **file** (read in the tab, never uploaded; CRC-32 streams so file size doesn't matter), with a paste-the-published-checksum box that states whether they match rather than leaving you to compare 64 characters by eye. Entirely offline, no network at any point
- [Assistant](/assistant): a free in-app AI guide — ask what any app does or how to do a task, and it answers from a built-in knowledge base of the workspace and opens the right tool. It also acts on instructions typed in the chat ("open the timer", "go to PDF merge", "turn on dark mode", "open settings", "clear the chat"). No API key or account; it uses the browser's built-in on-device model when present, otherwise a bundled offline retrieval engine
- [Walkaround](/walkaround): a guided tour of any app in the workspace, for the things an app does not say about itself on arrival. Pick an app and it plays a short walkthrough of that one: each stop is a **tooltip anchored to a schematic of that app’s screen** — its header, its Apps button, its working area block by block, and its bottom tabs — saying where a control is and what it does, plus a **suggestion**: the shortcut, the combination or the caveat regular use does not turn up. Stops are reached with the arrow keys, by tapping a numbered pin on the drawing, or from a dot; the complete tour is also written out as text below the drawing, direction and suggestion in full, so nothing exists only inside a tooltip. It tours a *drawing* rather than the live app on purpose — nothing here reads or changes another app’s state, so a walkaround can never break the app it describes — and an **Open** button hands you over to the real one when you have read it. Finishing a tour ticks that app off in the picker, which is the only thing kept on the device (`sknotes:walk:`). Fully offline; every tour is bundled, with no network and no model involved
- [Scan](/scan): turn a photograph of a page into a PDF, entirely on this device. The step that makes it a scanner rather than a camera roll is **perspective correction**: you mark the page's four corners on the capture and the page is *flattened* — a homography computed from those corners and applied by inverse mapping with bilinear sampling — so a page shot at an angle comes out rectangular rather than merely cropped. Corners are draggable and also **keyboard-operable** (each is a focusable control the arrow keys nudge), because a four-corner drag otherwise has no route to the same result. Pages come from the rear camera at the highest resolution it will give, or from pictures already on the device (batch import, downscaled past 3000px so the warp stays fast). Four finishes: **Colour** as photographed, **Grey**, **Document** — a *local* threshold that estimates the lighting from a blurred copy and divides it out, so a page lit from one side does not come out half grey and half black, which is what a single global threshold does — and **Ink**, pure two-tone for line art and signatures. Pages can be rotated, reordered and deleted, then saved as a multi-page PDF at the scan's own size or fitted to A4, Letter or Legal (aspect ratio preserved, orientation matched per page, so a landscape receipt is not letterboxed). Built with pdf-lib in the browser; the camera is released the moment the app is left, and **nothing is stored at all** — pages live in memory until the PDF is saved, which is deliberate for the documents people actually scan
- [Wallet](/wallet): an expense tracker built around the only thing that decides whether one gets used — logging has to take about four seconds. Type an amount, tap a category, done: the date defaults to today, the note is optional, and the category and date persist between entries because the next one is usually the same kind on the same day. Amounts are held as **integer minor units** throughout, never floats, so no total can quietly drift by a paisa. **Log** shows the last fortnight grouped by day with income netted against spending. **Month** rolls the month up — spent, received, net, and mean spend per *day elapsed* rather than per day in the month (dividing by 31 on the 3rd is a reassuring, meaningless number) — with a ranked category breakdown and share bars, a day-by-day chart, an optional monthly target that reports rather than nags, and a CSV export with properly quoted notes. **Split** divides a bill by weighted shares and assigns **every last minor unit**: shares are floored and the remainder handed out largest-fraction-first, so the parts sum exactly to the total and the app says who absorbed the odd unit — then settles the group in the fewest transfers by matching largest debtor to largest creditor. No account, no bank connection, nothing uploaded; splits are not persisted, because a split is a conversation rather than a record
- [Voice Memos](/voice): record a memo and, if you want, transcribe it as you speak — because audio is unsearchable, which is why voice memos pile up unlistened everywhere else. Recording uses MediaRecorder with echo cancellation, noise suppression and auto gain, mono at 32 kbps (speech gains nothing from stereo), with a live level meter, pause and resume, a ten-minute cap that stops a forgotten recording, and a discard that throws it away. Transcription uses the browser's own speech recognition, restarted automatically when it stops on its own — which it does, silently, mid-recording — so a transcript does not quietly end three minutes into a ten-minute memo. Memos are titled inline, played with the browser's native audio control, downloadable as .webm/.m4a, and **searched by transcript**, which is what makes an old memo findable. Audio is kept on the device under a size cap; past it the **oldest audio is cleared and its transcript kept**, which is the right thing to lose first. One caveat, stated in the app beside the switch rather than buried: recording never leaves the device, but transcription is performed by the browser's speech service — in Chrome that means the audio goes to Google — so it is **off by default**
- [Convert](/convert): the number counterpart to Text Kit. **Units** across twelve categories — length, weight, temperature, volume, area, speed, data (both decimal kB/MB and binary KiB/MiB), time, pressure, energy, fuel and angle — with the two non-linear cases handled properly rather than bent into a factor: temperature carries an offset as well as a scale, and litres-per-100km is the *reciprocal* of kilometres-per-litre. Under the answer, the same input in **every other unit of the category**, because the unit you wanted is often one you did not think to select, plus the rate ("1 m = 3.2808 ft"), which is the fact worth remembering. The unit side is unconditionally offline. **Money** converts at European Central Bank reference rates through this site's own server route, across 30+ currencies, with an at-a-glance table for 1/10/100/1000 — and because the ECB publishes once a working day and the last table is kept for offline use, **the publish date is shown as part of the answer**, so a Friday rate seen on Monday is never mistaken for a live one
- [API Client](/apiclient): build an HTTP request, send it, read the reply. Methods GET/POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE/HEAD/OPTIONS, header rows that keep their order and can be switched off without being deleted, JSON/text/form bodies with the Content-Type filled in only when you have not set one yourself, a saved collection, and the equivalent **curl command** with shell-safe quoting. The response viewer shows status, time and size, pretty-prints JSON while keeping the raw bytes one tab away (the difference between the two is sometimes the bug), and lists every response header. Two things it is honest about rather than mysterious: the request is made by **this site's server**, because a browser cannot call an API that has not opted into CORS — so **private addresses are refused explicitly** (localhost, RFC1918, carrier-grade NAT, link-local, IPv4-mapped IPv6 and the cloud metadata endpoint, checked against every address the hostname *resolves* to rather than against the string, with a port allowlist and no redirect following) and the app points you at the curl line for anything local; and because what people send to APIs includes bearer tokens, **the request history is never written to disk** — it lives in memory until the tab closes. The saved collection and the draft are local
- [Snippets](/snippets): a searchable library for the code you keep looking up. One flat list and one search box — no folders, no categories, because a snippet library fails by being slower to search than rewriting the thing. The single query spans titles, tags, languages and bodies, with `#tag` and `lang:go` to narrow, and every term must match so adding a word narrows the list. Copy is on every card, not behind a detail view. Fifteen languages are syntax-highlighted by a small built-in tokeniser rather than a highlighting library (which would cost more than the whole app), and the language is guessed from the first paste. Sort by last edited, most used, title or newest; duplicate, tag (up to eight), and edit with a preview toggle. Entirely local, which is the point rather than a limitation: the snippets people keep are connection strings, auth headers and internal endpoints, and this is the snippet manager that cannot leak them because it has nowhere to send them
- [Markdown](/markdown): write markdown with a live preview. Headings, bold/italic/strikethrough, inline and fenced code, links, images, bare-URL autolinking, tables with alignment, blockquotes containing their own blocks, nested lists, task lists and rules — plus **Mermaid diagrams**, with the diagram engine downloaded only when a document actually contains one, so opening the app to type a paragraph costs nothing. A table of contents, live word count and reading time, and three layouts (write, split, read) with split hidden on narrow screens, because two 180px columns serve neither writing nor reading. Exports as **.md** or as a **standalone HTML file** with its styles inlined and no external requests, so it opens the same offline, on a phone, or attached to an email. The parser produces a **tree of typed nodes, never an HTML string**, and the preview renders it as React elements — so there is no sanitiser to get wrong, pasted markdown containing a script tag is inert by construction, and `javascript:` link targets render as plain text rather than as anchors. One document, deliberately: it is the scratchpad you write a README or meeting notes in and then export. Fully offline
- [Chrono](/chrono): the questions about time a clock cannot answer. **Cron** explains any five-field expression in plain English (collapsing an even step back into "every 15 minutes" rather than listing four numbers), names the five fields under what you typed so a syntax error is locatable, and — the check that catches a misunderstanding rather than a typo — lists **the next 5, 10 or 25 times it fires** as real local dates. It handles `@daily`-style shorthands, month and day names, Sunday as 0 or 7, and spells out cron's most surprising rule: when both day-of-month and day-of-week are restricted they are **either/or**, not both. An expression that parses but never fires (30 February) is reported as such rather than hanging the tab. **Stamp** reads a pasted timestamp or date and shows it in every form — local, ISO local, ISO UTC, Unix seconds and milliseconds, RFC 2822, day-of-year and ISO week, optionally in a second time zone — and states out loud how it read a bare number ("read as seconds since 1970"), because a ten-digit number could be seconds or truncated milliseconds and guessing wrong lands you decades away with no visible error. Empty means *now*, and only then does the clock tick. **Length** parses "1h 20m", "90" (minutes) or "01:20:30", reports a mistyped unit instead of counting it as zero, shows the duration in every unit, and adds it to a moment. Entirely on this device
- [Contrast](/contrast): where Color Lens *reads* colour, this answers whether your colours work. **Check** grades a foreground/background pair against every WCAG 2.2 level (AA and AAA, body and large text, UI and graphics) with a live sample at the three sizes the thresholds are actually written for — and when body text fails it offers **the nearest passing shade**, found by walking lightness in linear-light space so the hue and saturation the design chose are kept. The verdict is carried by a word and an icon, never by colour alone, since a contrast tool signalling only in colour would be its own worst example. **Ramp** builds a 50–950 tonal scale from one colour, mixed towards white and black in *linear light* so the steps look evenly spaced rather than bunching at the pale end, with each step's contrast against white, black and its own best text colour on the row — then exports as CSS custom properties, **Tailwind v4 `@theme` entries** (not a v4-incompatible JS config), SCSS or JSON. **Vision** simulates protanopia, deuteranopia, tritanopia and achromatopsia with the cone-space matrices applied in linear RGB, and rather than leaving you to spot the problem it **measures every pair after simulation and lists the ones that collapse together** — because with eight colours on screen "look carefully" is not a check. Entirely local, and built on the same colour primitives the workspace's own theme picker grades with, so a verdict here and one there can never disagree
- [Satellite Map](/satellite): look at any place on Earth from above, with what is genuinely current drawn on top. Three base layers — **Satellite** (photographic imagery, Esri/Maxar World Imagery, to zoom 19), **Streets** and **Terrain** — with an optional transparent sheet of place names and borders over any of them. Over that, one of two **current** layers: **rain radar** from RainViewer, re-published about every ten minutes as a run of time-stamped frames covering the last couple of hours (plus a nowcast projected ahead when one is published), or **today from orbit** — NASA GIBS's true-colour mosaic of the whole planet, rebuilt daily, stepping back through the last seven days. Either is played as an animation or scrubbed by hand, and the app states in plain words how old the newest *measured* frame is and marks projected frames as forecast rather than letting them pass as observations. Important, and stated in the app itself: the base imagery is a **photograph months or years old**, because no public service streams the ground in real time — what is current here is the radar, NASA's daily pass, and the device's own position. **Street View**: a one-tap link to the ground-level panorama for a point — from the map's own controls, from any pin, or from where you are standing (opened facing the way the device says you are facing, where it knows). This is a link out to Google's Maps URLs API rather than an in-app viewer, and deliberately: every keyless open source of street-level imagery was measured first, and KartaView — the open one — returns nothing within five kilometres of Kochi, Trivandrum, Bengaluru, Delhi, Mumbai, Berlin or New York. An in-app viewer on it would answer "no imagery here" almost everywhere. Only the coordinates travel with the link, and no imagery service is contacted from the page itself. **Find** searches places by name through OpenStreetMap's Nominatim geocoder (only when submitted — never per keystroke), resolves pasted coordinates entirely on the device, finds where you are, reverse-geocodes what is under the crosshair, and keeps places (name and coordinates only) in this browser. **Locating** is offered in three places — the map's corner control, Find, and Live — but a single GPS watch backs all of them; asking to be located also takes you there — the first fix centres the map and zooms in far enough to recognise the street, rather than acquiring a position in silence — and the map control then becomes the follow toggle. Dragging the map turns following off rather than snatching the view back, and giving up on locating discards the pending jump so a late fix cannot yank the map away. **Live** watches the device's GPS with a marker and an accuracy circle, reports speed, heading, altitude and fix age; the position is never stored and never sent anywhere, and leaving the app ends the watch. The map is a hand-written canvas tile renderer — pan by drag or arrow keys, zoom by wheel, pinch, double-click or the +/− controls, with a latitude-aware scale bar and full attribution, and coarser tiles borrowed as a placeholder while sharper ones load. Needs a connection for map tiles, place search and the live layers; kept places and your last view are held locally. No API key is used anywhere in it

## Offline / low-bandwidth behaviour

- Works 100% offline after the first visit. A service worker (/sw.js) precaches every app
  route's HTML, then stores every file in the build manifest (/precache-manifest.json) —
  which includes the code-split chunk for every app. So one online visit
  to any single page is enough for every deep link (e.g. /todos, /pdfeditor) to cold-load
  with no connection, not just the app that was open when the network dropped.
- An app whose code is somehow not stored (a connection lost mid-download, or a deploy
  that renamed the chunks) shows a "not saved for offline use yet" panel with a way to
  open another app, rather than failing the whole page.
- Users can force or clear the download from Settings → Offline ("Save all apps for
  offline"). Automatic precaching is skipped on metered or 2g-class connections; the
  explicit save from Settings runs regardless.
- Offline is detected from what requests actually do, not only `navigator.onLine`, so the
  offline states also appear behind a captive portal or a dead uplink that the browser
  still reports as being online.
- On a weak connection the app serves saved content rather than stalling: navigations
  fall back to the cached shell after 3.5s, API responses after 6s.
- Fully offline: Sketch Notes, PDF Editor, Image Studio, Board, Todos, Reminders, Timer,
  System Info, Resource Monitor, Text Kit (pure local text operations), QR Codes, Handoff (both entirely local — a camera and a
  screen, never a network), File Drop on one network ("this network only" contacts nothing
  outside it; only the "anywhere" mode needs internet), Nearby Devices (the discovery APIs are local; only cast-display detection
  needs the local network), Morse Code, Sound Meter, Color Lens, Malayalam transliteration +
  keyboard, on-device Translate, Assistant, Walkaround, Scan, Wallet, Snippets, Markdown
  (Mermaid included, once its engine has been stored), Chrono, Contrast, Convert's unit side,
  Voice Memos' recording, and World Clock apart from its News tab —
  clocks, time zones and every country detail are computed and bundled locally, and
  country flags fall back to the ISO code when the flag image has not been cached.
- Needs a connection: Streams (both finding and playing come from YouTube; a station
  opened earlier still lists what it found, but nothing plays offline), News and World Clock headlines (previously loaded headlines still
  open from cache), online
  translation (previously translated phrases still open), Malayalam handwriting
  recognition, Speed Test, public-IP lookup, Convert's currency rates (the last published
  table is kept and shown with its date), Voice Memos' transcription (recording still works
  offline; only the speech recognition needs the network), and the API Client (every request
  is relayed by this site's server, so it cannot work offline at all). Each of these states
  this in the UI when offline instead of failing silently.
- Installable as a PWA (manifest at /manifest.webmanifest, with app shortcuts).

## Settings

Opened from the bottom of the app launcher; every preference applies to all apps and is
stored on the device.

- Theme: twenty-four built-in palettes, grouped by base. Light — Light, Ocean, Sky, Mint,
  Forest, Sunset, Clay, Sand, Olive, Rose, Grape, Lavender, Slate. Dark — Dark, Midnight,
  Carbon, Abyss, Matrix, Nebula, Ember, Wine, Mocha, Arctic, Noir (Noir is pure black, for
  OLED screens). Every palette holds WCAG AA contrast on the text it carries.
  Custom themes: up to twelve of your own, each built from a base (light or dark), an
  accent and a background colour — the rest of the palette is derived from those, and the
  editor shows the accent's live contrast ratio against the background so a theme you make
  stays readable. Saved themes can be renamed, re-coloured and deleted. Everything is
  stored on the device.
- Interface: the workspace's shape, separate from its colour. Five styles — Glass
  (translucent frosted panels over an ambient wash, the default), Solid (opaque cards, no
  blur), Soft (large round corners, wide diffuse shadow), Sharp (square corners, tight
  shadow) and Outline (borders instead of shadows). Plus three densities — Compact, Cosy,
  Roomy — which scale padding, gaps and control sizes together. Style and density are
  independent, and both are stored on the device.
- Pointer: replaces the mouse cursor workspace-wide. System (the device's own) plus
  thirteen drawn presets — Arrow, Chevron, Hand, Crosshair, Dot, Ring, Pen, Pencil,
  Brush, Sparkle, Star, Heart and Pixel — each in four sizes (Small to Huge) and
  coloured by the theme, by the accent, or by a colour you pick. A pointer of your own can be made
  from any image file or emoji, rendered on the device (nothing is uploaded), with its
  hotspot at the top-left or the centre. Touch input and the drawing/text cursors are
  unaffected.
- Sound: interface sounds, off by default — switch them on in Settings → Sound, which also
  previews the start-up chime. Deliberately plain — three notes when the workspace opens,
  one soft tone whenever you arrive somewhere, and nothing that is not a note. Every app has
  its own note (its place in the app catalog) and so does every page inside an app (its
  place in that app's tab bar), so moving forward through a tab bar rises in pitch and
  moving back falls. Opening the app switcher sounds an open fifth — the one chord, for the
  one place that isn't somewhere you have arrived. Every tone is drawn from a single C major
  pentatonic scale, so any two in a row are consonant even when one is still ringing. All
  synthesized in the browser (no audio files), always quiet, and nothing else in the
  workspace makes a sound unless asked (Timer alarms, Reminder alerts, Morse tones).
  Browsers block audio until the page has been interacted with, so the start-up chime is
  skipped on a cold load; Settings has a button to play it.
- Offline: save every app to the device, or clear what's stored.
- Recently deleted: notes, tasks, reminders and board sections you delete are kept for 30 days
  and can be restored from here, so a slip is recoverable. Restoring puts the item back where it
  came from and reloads. Very large items aren't kept, and the app says so at the time rather
  than implying a safety net that isn't there. Nothing else — an emptied canvas, a cleared
  history — is kept.
- Data: the workspace's only door in and out. **Save a backup** writes everything this
  browser holds — notes, tasks, reminders, boards, timers and preferences — as a single
  .zip containing a plain backup.json (a flat map of the very storage keys the apps read,
  so an old backup keeps working after an app changes how it stores things). **Restore
  from a backup** accepts that .zip or a bare .json, shows what is inside it per app
  before writing anything, then offers "add to this browser" (overwrite only what the
  backup covers) or "replace everything" (also delete what the backup does not mention).
  **Ask to keep it** requests persistent storage so the browser stops treating the
  workspace as evictable. **Erase all workspace data** clears every key, behind a confirm
  step. Nothing is uploaded at any point: the file is written by the browser and read back
  by the browser.

## Notes

- No accounts, no server storage — data is kept on the device in IndexedDB (with
  localStorage as a fallback, and an automatic one-time migration from it). That store is
  measured against the origin's real quota rather than localStorage's ~5 MB, is readable
  by the service worker, and never leaves the device. Settings → Data exports and restores
  it as a file.
- Command palette: Ctrl/⌘ + K from any app opens one search field over the workspace,
  covering every app, every PDF section, every theme and the settings overlays — and **the
  contents of your own data**: note titles and note text, tasks and their notes, board sections
  and their rows, reminders, scanned QR codes and the Malayalam document, shown under "Found in
  your data" with the matching text in context. Opening a hit goes to the item, not just the app
  (a note opens; a board card is scrolled to and flashed). The search reads storage only after a
  few characters and only while the palette is open, and its readers are loaded on first use so
  they cost nothing at start-up; ↑/↓ moves,
  Enter opens, Esc closes. Anything it cannot match is offered to the Assistant instead.
  The app launcher has a search button that opens the same palette.
- Installed-app integration: OneApp registers as a file handler for PDFs, images and its
  own .json/.zip documents, so double-clicking one opens it in the right app (a PDF opened
  this way can be edited and saved straight back to the same file via the File System
  Access API). It is also a share target — sharing a file, a link or text to OneApp from
  another app routes it to the app that can use it, with the service worker receiving the
  share so the payload never reaches a server.
- Reminders while closed: with OneApp installed, a periodic background sync lets the
  service worker check for due reminders and fire them when no tab is open. The browser
  decides when to wake it, so a background alert can be late but never early and never
  twice; where it is unavailable the app says plainly that alerts arrive only while OneApp
  is open.
- Apps are switched from the launcher (the "Switch app" button in any app's header)
  without a page load; the URL still changes to that app's path, and the app's logo plays
  a brief opening animation over the new screen. Motion throughout the workspace is
  dropped when the browser asks for reduced motion.
- Loading the workspace plays a short opening animation: every app's chip converges into
  one point and the "One App" wordmark unfolds out of it. It is a flourish over an app that
  has already mounted, not a loading state — nothing waits on it.
- Device permissions are asked for only on the feature that needs one, and only from a
  click: notifications (Reminders), the microphone (Sound Meter) and the camera (Color
  Lens), and the per-device choosers in Nearby Devices (Bluetooth, USB, HID, serial —
  each granted one device at a time, by the browser, never by the page). Captured audio
  and video are analysed in memory and discarded — never recorded
  or transmitted — and the device is released as soon as the feature is done with it.
- Resource Monitor is the exception that proves the rule: it asks for camera, microphone,
  screen capture and location on purpose, so you can see what a site gets, and every one
  of them is held only while you leave it open and released the instant you press stop or
  switch apps. It is the one place to review all of the above in one list, per resource
  and per app.
